docs.title: Working notes
docs.text:
Notes on Linux internals, Rust, eBPF, and the parts of running infrastructure that only become obvious at 3am. Written while the details are still fresh, which means occasionally being wrong in public and correcting it later.

This is where the reasoning behind the opinions on helius.dk lives. If you want to know how I think before you email me, start here.

docs.title: Blackbox Linux — build notes
docs.text:
Working notes from building Blackbox Linux: an eBPF runtime visibility agent for Linux servers, written in Rust. Process-tree tracing, in-kernel filtering, a small declarative rule engine.

Not released yet

First public release targets December 2026. Until there is a tagged version and a public repository, everything here describes intent and work-in-progress, not shipped behaviour. If you are evaluating it for production, wait for the tag.

This section is the engineering diary — the decisions, the measurements, and the things that turned out to be wrong. The product page has the overview and architecture; this is where the reasoning lives.

docs.title: Why it is being built in the open
docs.text: The claim Blackbox makes is that you should not run an agent you cannot audit as root on every host you own. That claim is only worth anything if the work itself is inspectable — including the parts that did not work. So the notes go up as they happen rather than being tidied into a launch post.

docs.title: What gets written about here
docs.text:
• Kernel work — probe attachment, CO-RE, what verifier rejections actually meant, why a given hook was the wrong one.
  • Filtering — the cost of an event that reaches userspace versus one dropped in-kernel, measured rather than assumed.
  • Correlation — turning a flat stream of fork/execve/exit into process trees a human can read, and where that gets expensive.
  • Overhead — honest numbers on real workloads, including the cases where the overhead was worse than expected.

docs.title: Follow along
docs.text: There is no mailing list. Posts land in the blog, and the repository goes public with the first release. If you have a use case that should shape it — particularly an environment where existing agents were too expensive or too opaque — email me and tell me about it while the design is still soft.

docs.title: The case against a service mesh
docs.text:
You probably want mTLS and retries. You probably do not want another control plane.

A mesh solves real problems. It also adds a sidecar to every pod, a control plane to upgrade, and a new class of outage that looks exactly like a network partition.

docs.title: cgroup v2 memory limits are not what you think
docs.text:
memory.max is not a hard ceiling on RSS, and the OOM killer is not the only failure mode.

A container that never gets OOM-killed can still spend most of its life in reclaim, doing almost no useful work while looking perfectly healthy to your orchestrator.

docs.title: Rebuilding helius.dk
docs.text: For a few years helius.dk was a MkDocs blog and nothing else — Solana tooling, Rust performance notes, kernel debugging. It has now grown a front end, because the consulting side needed somewhere to point people that was not a list of posts about ring buffers.

docs.title: What changed
docs.text:
The marketing site is Astro and owns the root domain. The blog is still MkDocs and now lives here at /blog. They are two independent static builds stitched together at deploy time:

mkdocs build -d public/blog   →  Astro copies public/ verbatim
astro build                   →  dist/  →  GitHub Pages

Neither half knows the other exists. That is deliberate: I can rebuild the blog without touching the site, and the site has no content pipeline reaching into Markdown it does not own. The cost is that a broken Python step fails the whole deploy, which is a trade I will take for the isolation.

The old post URLs are gone

The previous blog served posts from the domain root. Those paths now 404 rather than redirect. That was a deliberate call and it does throw away whatever ranking those pages had — if you were linking to one, that link is dead and I am not going to pretend otherwise.

docs.title: What the site is for
docs.text:
Helius does DevOps engineering: CI/CD, Kubernetes, infrastructure as code, observability, Linux hardening, performance work. All of it with open-source tooling, all of it committed to repositories the client owns.

The whole argument is on the pledge page, and it comes down to one test: a month after I stop working with you, is anything degraded? If the answer could be yes, I built the wrong thing.

docs.title: What lands in December
docs.text:
Blackbox Linux — an eBPF runtime visibility agent for Linux servers, written in Rust. Process-tree tracing, in-kernel filtering so uninteresting events never cost you anything, and a small declarative rule engine.

It exists because runtime security on Linux is mostly sold as closed agents licensed per host, and an agent you cannot audit has no business running as root on your servers.

It is not released yet. First public release targets December 2026, and until there is a tagged version, treat everything written about it as intent rather than documentation.

docs.title: Housekeeping
docs.text:
Posts here are in English only. The marketing site is bilingual (English and Danish); the blog is not, because maintaining translated technical writing is a commitment I would rather not make badly.

More to come — mostly eBPF, mostly Rust, occasionally a post-mortem where I was the cause.

docs.title: nftables for people who knew iptables
docs.text:
The mental model changed more than the syntax did, and that is the part that bites.

Translating your iptables rules one-for-one into nft syntax will produce a working ruleset and a deeply confusing one. Sets and maps are the point.

docs.title: Postgres connection pooling, measured
docs.text:
We tried four pool sizes on real traffic. The best one was smaller than everybody guessed.

The instinct is to raise max_connections until the errors stop. What actually happens is that the database spends its time context-switching instead of answering queries.

docs.title: Reading kernel ring buffers without losing events
docs.text:
A ring buffer that silently drops events is worse than no telemetry at all, because you will trust it.

The BPF_MAP_TYPE_RINGBUF docs tell you the happy path. They do not tell you what happens when userspace falls behind, which is the only case that matters in production.

docs.title: Signing container images without a key server
docs.text:
Keyless signing removes the one piece of infrastructure nobody wanted to run.

Long-lived signing keys need storage, rotation, and an owner. Workload identity gives you an attestable signature without any of the three.

docs.title: What perf tells you that Prometheus cannot
docs.text:
Metrics tell you a service is slow. A flamegraph tells you which function to open.

Application metrics are aggregate by construction. When the aggregate says 'slower since Tuesday' you need something that can point at a line of code.

docs.title: Why your p99 is a lie
docs.text:
Averaging percentiles across instances produces a number that is not a percentile of anything.

If you are computing p99 per pod and then averaging, you are not measuring the 99th percentile. You are measuring a quantity with no statistical meaning that happens to look reassuring on a dashboard.

docs.title: Snippets
docs.text:
Short things worth writing down once so I stop re-deriving them at 3am. No narrative, no build-up — the command, what it does, and the caveat.

Longer reasoning lives in posts. Everything here is open source and copy-pasteable.

docs.title: Find what a process is actually waiting on
docs.text:
# Live syscall latency histogram for one PID, no restart, no instrumentation.
sudo bpftrace -e '
  tracepoint:raw_syscalls:sys_enter /pid == '"$PID"'/ { @s[tid] = nsecs; }
  tracepoint:raw_syscalls:sys_exit  /pid == '"$PID"' && @s[tid]/ {
    @us[ksym(args->id)] = hist((nsecs - @s[tid]) / 1000); delete(@s[tid]);
  }'

Run it for 30 seconds before theorising. The answer is usually one syscall you were not thinking about.

docs.title: Which files does this service open most?
docs.text:
Good for finding filter candidates before you turn on verbose auditing.

sudo timeout 60s strace -f -qq -e trace=openat -p "$(pgrep -d, -f php-fpm)" 2>&1 \
  | sed -nE 's/.*openat\(.*"([^"]+)".*/\1/p' \
  | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -30

strace costs real performance — do this on one host, not the fleet.

docs.title: Postgres: find the unindexed query before adding cache
docs.text:
SELECT calls, round(mean_exec_time::numeric, 1) AS avg_ms,
       round(total_exec_time::numeric) AS total_ms, query
  FROM pg_stat_statements
 WHERE query NOT ILIKE '%pg_stat%'
 ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC
 LIMIT 15;

Sort by total time, not mean. A 4ms query run 900k times beats a 2s query run twice, and only one of them is worth your afternoon.

docs.title: Systemd unit that actually restarts on failure
docs.text:
[Service]
Restart=always
RestartSec=2
# Without these two, repeated crashes hit the default burst limit and
# systemd gives up silently — the unit sits in "failed" until someone looks.
StartLimitIntervalSec=0

# Kill the whole cgroup, not just the main pid.
KillMode=control-group
TimeoutStopSec=30

docs.title: nftables: default-deny that does not lock you out
docs.text:
# Validate BEFORE loading. `nft -c` parses without applying.
sudo nft -c -f /etc/nftables.conf && sudo nft -f /etc/nftables.conf

If you are applying over SSH, wrap it so a mistake self-reverts:

sudo systemd-run --on-active=120 --timer-property=AccuracySec=1s \
  nft flush ruleset
# You now have 2 minutes to confirm you can still connect.
# Still connected? Cancel it:  sudo systemctl stop run-r*.timer

docs.title: kubectl: what is actually eating the node
docs.text:
kubectl get pods -A -o custom-columns=\
'NS:.metadata.namespace,NAME:.metadata.name,'\
'CPU_REQ:.spec.containers[*].resources.requests.cpu,'\
'MEM_REQ:.spec.containers[*].resources.requests.memory,NODE:.spec.nodeName' \
  --field-selector spec.nodeName="$NODE" --sort-by=.metadata.namespace

Requests, not usage — this is what the scheduler reserved, which is what makes a node "full" while top looks idle.

docs.title: Reproducible container digest in CI
docs.text:
# Never deploy a tag. Tags move; digests do not.
DIGEST=$(docker buildx imagetools inspect "$IMAGE:$TAG" \
  --format '{{ "{{" }}.Manifest.Digest{{ "}}" }}')
kubectl set image deploy/app "app=$IMAGE@$DIGEST"
